questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have been to Berlin many times before, and wanted to go somewhere in Germany, so it made sense to choose what seemed somehow familiar in its newness.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is one of the best experiences in my life, and I would do it again if I could.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I had researched quite a lot before going, reading all on KUs website and been in touch with the exchange team at my institute, so I felt somewhat prepared - but of course there were surprises, confusing bureaucracy and stuff that is just impossible to know beforehand: I think the most important thing is to seek out the information, that seems important for you upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were introdays and also a very good and present counselor on the uni, if I had questions apart from the information everyone was given.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It is very difficult to figure out the ECTS and course-granting system in berlin, as it is so different from ours and very analogue in a sense - you can always speak with the professor, make your own deals on points and exams, and they are very willing to help you out and make it work: It is just important to talk to them, ask questions and accept the initial confusion.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used my network in Denmark, got my friends and parents to ask if anyone had connections in Berlin, and was lucky to find a room to rent. I would definitely recommend the facebook group 'danskere i berlin' and just reach out - you might be lucky!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I think there are multiple ways to do an exchange - I was also there a lot for the city, so i prioritized living closer to city center, and further from the university, which meant a daily commute but to be honest it was never anything I regretted: It takes a bit of time to get used to the bigger distances, but then it is also cozy and I just read most of the time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There aren't enough dorms for everyone, and they are quite far - both from uni and even further from the city. I heard from some that was living there, that it can be rather nice, since all your neighbours are students, but I preferred finding an apartment.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I remember it being difficult: everything with registering and finding my way around the new systems were a bit challenging, but I managed with a lot of patience, and asking for help here and there, especially the other students and my institute counselor were good.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't remember exactly, but since I had the language course before the semester, everything went a bit smoother, being already part of the system and familiar with the uni.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The other students, a counselor and an exchange office for broader questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very confused by the classes available and how many I wanted, so my registration process was a bit confusing I'll admit: In the end I was very happy with how it worked out, but maybe I would now prioritize classes where I didn't have to write a take home exam - at least in all of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I don't know, it depends a lot on how you want your exchange: I had very few courses, to have more time during the mobility, but that means I have to write three quite big exams. Maybe it would have been better having a class with credits just for participation. And I have heard very good about the JFK institute, though I didn't have any subjects there myself.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It wasn't as high a level as KU, I felt - not as much reading at least. I think my experience was that the open discussions were valued higher, sometimes taking time away from the texts or the curriculum, which is both a nice thing as people get really good at voicing opinions and finding arguments, but also I had the feeling that a lot of the discussions were based on more individual and personal experiences, and not so much on theory or considered in the perspective of theory. I missed that sometimes.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had a mixture of BA and MA courses, but it was never a problem I think. They were very different levels and reading amounts, but I enjoyed it. I would say go for what you think sounds interesting, and maybe attend more classes than you need the first week, just to get a feeling of the professor's style and the subject before choosing.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I like it at KU with the lecture and the seminair going hand in hand, and I sometimes missed the very informed discussions that could create: My professors were very good at creating an open forum and opening up for the discussions which was very fun to try though!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Documental poetry 
Listening to water (and other voices)
Transcreation
Neue deutschsprachige Literatur (von Berlin aus) gelesen

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think a lot of them are not repeated - the 'Listening to water'-course was taught by a guest professor, and I would definitely recommend applying for those (I think it's quite early, maybe the beginning of march)! My experience was that the students and the professor gave more of themselves.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not really any, I think - I had saved some money and prepared to spend some more, being away and everything.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food, restaurants, activities and everything was in general cheaper than in Copenhagen. I paid a lot in rent, but it was a choice to invest in a safe, spacious and good base.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is a lot! I went to free croquis at the arts uni, yoga and dance in the uni sport - I feel like everything was possible.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is unisport, and a lot of events for erasmus students

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think some of the erasmus events were rather interesting, and I would definitely recommend the croquis if you like drawing - its a nice, non-binding opportunity to leave your head a little.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Berlin is full of possibilities - it draws a lot more known theorists and artists than Copenhagen, so keep an eye open, cause I missed a lot due to general distræthed:)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy actually: I arrived a month before the language course started, to get some time for myself and get to know the city and I really enjoyed having had some time, cause everything seemed so much more relaxed and familiar.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I think be open and ready to talk to your classmates, and make some connections there. It is definitely easier to connect with the other exchange students, but in general I found people rather open and ready to talk.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I don't think there was any - I wish now, that I had been better at just speaking german in my everyday life and not letting the shyness stop me: that's maybe the most challenging, not to switch to english because it is easier. 
I think sometimes it can be difficult to ignore the pressure of partying and having the most fun all the time, but I think I just gave up on that, and tried to listen to what I wanted, and that helped me a lot, even though it might sound like a stupid advice.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the diversity and the openness - I felt initially welcome in a different way, and with stuff happening all the time anyways, it seems to me more okay to just make it to the things that I found most important or interesting.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Have time to just get lost in the streets, be alone a bit and just walk around, landing in the new surroundings.
I would always prioritize a safe and cozy home, because I need a good base to recharge and find energy. 
Don't worry too much about all the uni bureaucracy, it will solve itself, if you talk and ask for the help you need: It just cannot be solved beforehand or at the same time.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep an eye out for the talks hosted by the different universities, some real stars come by sometimes! And find the counselor at your receiving institute, they are usually very helpful, when it comes to figuring out the confusing system of german uni administration.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know a lot of lovely people, trying out my own boundaries and discovering another city that I found to be a home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: At some point I found it very difficult to be so far away from everything I knew, and when I had to go back to DK, I found it very difficult to leave all of that which I had just come to know.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Just get going, I think its a great experience to get a bit outside of DK.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
